continuum-charts publishes three Helm charts for deploying Continuum on Kubernetes, served as a standard Helm chart repository via GitHub Pages.
Project Continuum is split across several focused repositories under the projectcontinuum-org GitHub organization — not a monorepo. Each one can be built and released independently.
continuum-feature-ai provides nodes for training and fine-tuning LLMs directly inside workflow graphs. Ships as a Spring Boot worker with an auto-managed Python virtual environment for ML execution.
continuum-feature-base ships 16 production-ready nodes for data transformation, filtering, aggregation, REST integration, scripting, and anomaly detection.

continuum-feature-cheminformatics ships 38 production-grade cheminformatics nodes across 10 categories, powered by RDKit. Built for computational chemistry, medicinal chemistry, and drug discovery teams who need scalable, reproducible molecular processing pipelines — parse, standardize, fingerprint, filter, react, and visualize molecules at scale.
continuum-feature-knime runs KNIME workflows (.knwf) on Continuum.

The continuum-local-setup repo gives you a single docker compose up that launches the complete Project Continuum stack — infrastructure services, platform backend, browser IDE, and feature workers — all wired together and ready to go.

Project Continuum is an open-source, browser-native visual workflow platform — inspired by KNIME, built for the cloud. You design workflows as a drag-and-drop graph of nodes, and the platform runs them durably: a crashed worker, a dead Kafka broker, or a dropped connection doesn't lose your progress.

All data passed between workflow nodes is Apache Parquet (Snappy-compressed, Avro schema DataRow) — not JSON. This keeps data columnar, compressed, and query-ready from the moment it leaves a node. Apache ParquetSnappyAvro schema DataRow ✍️Writing NodeOutputWriter.OutputPortWriter writes rows to the node's output port(s). 📖Reading NodeInputReader reads rows from each connected input port. 🏷️File names Output files are named output.{portId}.parquet; input files input.{portId}.parquet. 🗂️Staging Files are staged in a local cache path before upload to (or after download from) MinIO, the platform's S3-compatible object store. Mix and match workers Because every node reads and writes the same Parquet/Avro format regardless of which worker or language implements it, nodes written in different feature repos — base analytics, cheminformatics, AI/ML — can be freely wired together in the same workflow graph.

Every workflow node is defined inside a feature worker — an independent service (e.g. continuum-feature-base, continuum-feature-ai, continuum-feature-cheminformatics, or your own) built with the continuum-worker-springboot-starter. Workers register their nodes centrally so the orchestration service knows which worker to dispatch each node to.

Every node: Is annotated @ContinuumNode (not just @Component) — enforced at build time by a Gradle validation task and at startup by the node activity handler. Extends ProcessNodeModel (data nodes) or TriggerNodeModel (source nodes). Overrides inputPorts, outputPorts, and metadata (as ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData). Implements execute() — the simple overload for most nodes, or the ExecutionContext overload for nodes that need credentials. MyNodeModel.kt @ContinuumNode class MyNodeModel : ProcessNodeModel() { override val inputPorts = mapOf("input" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(...)) override val outputPorts = mapOf("output" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(...)) override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData(...) override fun execute( properties: Map<String, Any>?, inputs: Map<String, NodeInputReader>, nodeOutputWriter: NodeOutputWriter, nodeProgressCallback: NodeProgressCallback, executionContext: ExecutionContext // only needed for credential access ) { /* ... */ } } Node documentation is auto-loaded from resources/<package>/<ClassName>.doc.md on startup.

At startup, each worker publishes its available nodes to Kafka so the platform can build a central registry of "which node lives on which worker": On ApplicationReadyEvent, the worker iterates every ContinuumNodeModel bean it has. For each node, it builds a FeatureRegistrationRequest — containing nodeId (fully-qualified class name), workerId, featureId, taskQueue, a JSON nodeManifest (ports, schemas, title, icon), and the node's documentation markdown — and publishes it to Kafka (Avro, keyed by nodeId). continuum-message-bridge consumes the message and performs an atomic upsert into the registered_nodes table. The orchestration service's InitializeActivity later queries this registry (via the API server) to resolve which task queue should run each node in a workflow. featureId is derived by stripping the trailing .node package segment from the class name, e.g. org.projectcontinuum.feature.analytics.node.CreateTableNodeModel → org.projectcontinuum.feature.analytics. nodeManifest is kept as an opaque JSON string (not typed Avro fields) so the schema stays forward-compatible as NodeData evolves. Registration is one message per node, enabling clean idempotent upserts, and extensions (a map<string>) is reserved for future fields without breaking schema compatibility.

documents.t: Nodes that need external secrets (API keys, DB passwords) don't receive them automatically: The node's propertiesUISchema declares a control with options.format = "credential" purely so continuum-workbench renders a credential picker in its config dialog — the backend doesn't read this schema. Inside execute(), the node reads its own properties to find the configured credential name, then calls executionContext.getCredential<T>(name). This fetches the credential on demand from continuum-credentials-server (GET /api/v1/credentials/{name}) and deserializes it into T, throwing if not found. Credentials are never stored in the workflow Credentials are fetched lazily, per execution — never bundled into the workflow definition or passed through Kafka.
Continuum is split into a browser frontend, a core backend (API server + Temporal orchestration), and independent feature workers that provide the actual workflow nodes.

You design a workflow in the browser (React Flow canvas) and hit Execute. continuum-api-server receives the REST call and starts a Temporal workflow (ContinuumWorkflow, on WORKFLOW_TASK_QUEUE). InitializeActivity resolves which task queue (= which worker) handles each node, via POST /api/v1/node-explorer/nodes/task-queues against the API server's node registry. For each DAG node, IContinuumNodeActivity.run() is dispatched to the resolved worker's task queue (ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE). The worker downloads input Parquet from MinIO, runs execute(), and uploads output Parquet. Nodes run in parallel where the DAG allows — ContinuumWorkflow waits for the first pending node to complete, then schedules newly unblocked nodes. Each node sends progress signals; ContinuumWorkflow publishes a WorkflowUpdateEvent to Kafka. continuum-message-bridge consumes the Kafka event and republishes it to Mosquitto (MQTT). The browser receives the update over MQTT-over-WebSocket and lights up the corresponding node in real time. The same flow as a sequence:

Crash-proof by design Temporal persists workflow state (in PostgreSQL) at every step. If a worker process dies mid-execution, the orchestration service simply redispatches the pending activity once a worker becomes available again — no data loss, no restart from scratch. This is the "crash-proof execution" promise: a failed Kafka broker, a restarted worker pod, or a dropped network connection doesn't lose workflow progress.

Three Temporal task queues coordinate the system: Queue Consumer Purpose WORKFLOW_TASK_QUEUE ContinuumWorkflow (orchestration service) Drives the DAG execution loop ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE ContinuumNodeActivity (feature workers) Runs individual node logic — name overridable per worker via continuum.core.worker.node-task-queue ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE_INITIALIZE InitializeActivity (orchestration service) Resolves node → task queue routing before dispatch See Node Model & Registration for how a worker's nodes end up in that registry in the first place, and Data Format for how data actually moves between nodes.

Continuum is designed to be extended by adding new workers, not modifying existing ones — see Node Model & Feature Registration for why that's safe to do independently. To build your own set of nodes, start from continuum-feature-template — a scaffold for a standalone Gradle project with the Spring Boot worker setup, Temporal registration, and @ContinuumNode conventions already wired up. tip The template builds against platform 0.0.20 out of the box and includes a Kotlin and a Java example node, CI/CD workflows, a Helm chart and a local Docker stack. Its README covers renaming it for your own feature. For a walkthrough of writing a node from scratch, see Create New Nodes. Once your worker is running and registering nodes, it can be deployed as an independent release into the same Kubernetes namespace as the core platform (see Deployment) — no changes to continuum-platform-core or any other feature repo required. For questions or to report issues, use the GitHub issue tracker on the core repo.

This guide walks you through building a feature worker with your own workflow node, from an empty folder to a passing build and a worker that registers its node with the platform. The running example is a Word Counter node that counts the words in a text column and appends the count as a new column. Kotlin + Gradle9 stepsPlatform 0.0.20 You need to know some Kotlin and Gradle. You don't need to know Temporal, Kafka or Spring internals; the Continuum Gradle plugins and the worker starter handle those. Versions used in this guide Verified against Continuum platform 0.0.20 (Spring Boot 4.0.6, Kotlin 2.2, Jackson 3, Gradle 8.14, JDK 21). Check Maven Central for the latest platform version, and use the same version everywhere in your project.

A feature worker is a small Gradle multi-project: continuum-feature-demo/ ├── settings.gradle.kts # plugin versions + module list ├── gradle.properties # continuumPlatformVersion, featureVersion ├── features/ │ └── continuum-feature-demo/ # library module: your node classes └── worker/ # thin Spring Boot app that hosts the nodes Feature modules (org.projectcontinuum.feature plugin) hold the node classes. They're plain libraries and can be published and reused. The worker module (org.projectcontinuum.worker plugin) is a Spring Boot app with no node logic of its own. It depends on your feature modules and on continuum-worker-springboot-starter. At startup the starter finds every @ContinuumNode bean, polls a Temporal task queue for node executions, and publishes one registration message per node to Kafka. See Node Model & Feature Registration for what happens after registration.

Requirement Notes JDK 21 Eclipse Temurin recommended. The plugins set a Java 21 toolchain. Gradle wrapper 8.14+ Older wrappers (for example 8.4) can't load the Spring Boot 4 Gradle plugin. Docker Only needed to run the worker against the local stack. You don't need a GitHub token. All Continuum artifacts and Gradle plugins are published to Maven Central.

Create the root project Create the feature module Write the node Add node documentation Write unit tests Create the worker module Build and test Run the worker against the local stack Ship it If something goes wrong along the way, see Troubleshooting.

Step 1 of 911% through the guide Create the folder and add a Gradle wrapper. If Gradle is installed, run gradle wrapper --gradle-version 8.14. Otherwise, copy gradlew, gradlew.bat and gradle/wrapper/ from an existing feature repo such as continuum-feature-base. gradle.properties repoName=your-org/continuum-feature-demo continuumPlatformVersion=0.0.20 featureVersion=0.0.1 # Spring Boot 4 pulls in a large Kotlin compiler jar; give the Gradle daemon enough heap. org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g continuumPlatformVersion selects the Gradle plugin version and the continuum-commons / continuum-worker-springboot-starter versions. featureVersion is your own version. repoName is used in published POM metadata and in the default container image name. settings.gradle.kts pluginManagement { val continuumPlatformVersion: String by settings repositories { mavenLocal() mavenCentral() gradlePluginPortal() } plugins { id("org.projectcontinuum.feature") version continuumPlatformVersion id("org.projectcontinuum.worker") version continuumPlatformVersion } } rootProject.name = "continuum-feature-demo" include(":features:continuum-feature-demo") include(":worker") The plugins are resolved from Maven Central, so mavenCentral() must be in pluginManagement.repositories, not only in gradlePluginPortal().

Step 2 of 922% through the guide features/continuum-feature-demo/build.gradle.kts plugins { id("org.projectcontinuum.feature") } group = "org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo" description = "Continuum Feature Demo — demo nodes" version = property("featureVersion").toString() continuum { continuumVersion.set(property("continuumPlatformVersion").toString()) } Always set continuumVersion If you leave out the continuum { } block, the plugin falls back to a built-in default version that is older than the plugin itself. Read the value from gradle.properties so plugins and libraries always match. The org.projectcontinuum.feature plugin applies Kotlin and Spring dependency management and adds these dependencies for you, so you don't declare them yourself: Spring Boot starter, web, actuator and autoconfigure continuum-commons kotlin-reflect and tools.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin Test: spring-boot-starter-test, kotlin-test-junit5, mockito-kotlin It also registers the validateContinuumNodeAnnotations task, which runs before classes. Add a dependencies { } block only for extra libraries your nodes need.

The worker finds your nodes through Spring Boot auto-configuration, so each feature module needs two small files. src/main/kotlin/org/projectcontinuum/feature/demo/AutoConfigure.kt package org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo import org.springframework.context.annotation.ComponentScan import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration @Configuration @ComponentScan class AutoConfigure src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo.AutoConfigure @ComponentScan with no arguments scans the package of AutoConfigure and its subpackages. If the imports file is missing or names the wrong class, the build still passes but the worker starts with none of your nodes.

Step 3 of 933% through the guide Put node classes in a .node subpackage. The platform derives your feature ID by removing the trailing .node segment from the class name. For example, org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo.node.WordCounterNodeModel gets the feature ID org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo. src/main/kotlin/org/projectcontinuum/feature/demo/node/WordCounterNodeModel.kt package org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo.node import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.annotation.ContinuumNode import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.exception.NodeRuntimeException import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.model.ContinuumWorkflowModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.node.ProcessNodeModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.protocol.progress.NodeProgressCallback import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeInputReader import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeOutputWriter import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory import org.springframework.http.MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper @ContinuumNode class WordCounterNodeModel( private val objectMapper: ObjectMapper ) : ProcessNodeModel() { companion object { private val LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(WordCounterNodeModel::class.java) private val WHITESPACE = Regex("\\s+") } // 1. Ports: the map keys ("data") are the port IDs used in execute() final override val inputPorts = mapOf( "data" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "input table", contentType = TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE) ) final override val outputPorts = mapOf( "data" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "table with word counts", contentType = TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE) ) // 2. Where the node appears in the workbench node explorer override val categories = listOf("Demo") // 3. JSON Schema for the node's properties val propertiesSchema: Map<String, Any> = objectMapper.readValue( """ { "type": "object", "properties": { "inputCol": { "type": "string", "title": "Input Column" }, "outputCol": { "type": "string", "title": "Output Column" }, "minWordLength": { "type": "integer", "title": "Minimum Word Length", "minimum": 1, "default": 1 } }, "required": ["inputCol", "outputCol"] } """.trimIndent(), object : TypeReference<Map<String, Any>>() {} ) // 4. JSON Forms UI schema: layout of the configuration dialog val propertiesUiSchema: Map<String, Any> = objectMapper.readValue( """ { "type": "VerticalLayout", "elements": [ { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/inputCol" }, { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/outputCol" }, { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/minWordLength" } ] } """.trimIndent(), object : TypeReference<Map<String, Any>>() {} ) // 5. Metadata: what the workbench and registry see override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData( id = this.javaClass.name, nodeModel = this.javaClass.name, title = "Word Counter", subTitle = "Count words per row", description = "Counts the words in a text column and appends the count as a new column", icon = """<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M4 6h16M4 12h10M4 18h6M18 14v6m-3-3h6"/></svg>""", inputs = inputPorts, outputs = outputPorts, properties = mapOf("inputCol" to "text", "outputCol" to "word_count", "minWordLength" to 1), propertiesSchema = propertiesSchema, propertiesUISchema = propertiesUiSchema ) // 6. The node's logic override fun execute( properties: Map<String, Any>?, inputs: Map<String, NodeInputReader>, nodeOutputWriter: NodeOutputWriter, nodeProgressCallback: NodeProgressCallback ) { val inputCol = properties?.get("inputCol") as String? ?: throw NodeRuntimeException(workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "inputCol is not provided") val outputCol = properties["outputCol"] as String? ?: throw NodeRuntimeException(workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "outputCol is not provided") val minWordLength = (properties["minWordLength"] as Number?)?.toInt() ?: 1 val reader = inputs["data"] ?: throw NodeRuntimeException( isRetriable = false, workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "Input port 'data' is not connected" ) val totalRows = reader.getRowCount() nodeOutputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("data").use { writer -> reader.use { var row = reader.read() var rowNumber = 0L while (row != null) { val text = row[inputCol]?.toString() ?: "" val count = text.trim().split(WHITESPACE).count { it.length >= minWordLength } writer.write(rowNumber, row.toMutableMap().apply { this[outputCol] = count }) rowNumber++ if (totalRows > 0) nodeProgressCallback.report((rowNumber * 100 / totalRows).toInt()) row = reader.read() } LOGGER.info("Counted words in $rowNumber rows") } } } }

Rule Why Annotate with @ContinuumNode, not @Component. @ContinuumNode makes the bean prototype-scoped, so each execution gets a fresh instance. The build fails if a node class is missing it (see Step 7). Extend ProcessNodeModel for nodes with inputs, or TriggerNodeModel for source nodes. TriggerNodeModel has only outputPorts and execute(properties, nodeOutputWriter). Set metadata.id and metadata.nodeModel to this.javaClass.name. The fully qualified class name is the node's identity in the registry and in saved workflows. Renaming or moving the class breaks existing workflows that use it. Use Jackson 3 imports (tools.jackson.*). Platform 0.0.20 is on Spring Boot 4 / Jackson 3. com.fasterxml.jackson.databind isn't on the classpath and won't compile. Take ObjectMapper as a constructor parameter. Spring injects it. In unit tests, pass jacksonObjectMapper().

metadata.properties holds the default values used when a node is dropped onto the canvas. Before execute() is called, ProcessNodeModel.run() validates the configured properties against propertiesSchema. Values that break required, type, minimum and similar rules fail the node before your code runs. You can still check values in execute() for clearer error messages. propertiesUISchema is a JSON Forms UI schema, used only by the workbench to draw the configuration dialog. For credential pickers (options.format = "credential"), see Credentials. You can try schemas in the JSON Forms playground before wiring them into a node.

inputs[portId] is a NodeInputReader. read() returns the next row as Map<String, Any>, or null at the end of the table. getRowCount() returns the total number of rows. nodeOutputWriter.createOutputPortWriter(portId) returns a writer. write(rowNumber, row) takes a Long row index starting at 0. Wrap both reader and writer in .use { }. The output Parquet file is only complete once the writer is closed. If an input port isn't connected, its key is missing from inputs. Cell values must be one of these types. Any other type makes write() throw IllegalArgumentException: Unsupported type. Kotlin type Stored as String application/vnd.continuum.x-string Int, Long application/vnd.continuum.x-int, x-long Float, Double application/vnd.continuum.x-float, x-double Boolean application/vnd.continuum.x-boolean List<*>, Map<*, *> application/json SVG org.w3c.dom.Document image/svg+xml Convert anything else first, for example call toString() on a LocalDate or BigDecimal. A null value can't be stored either: leave the key out instead.

Every node runs as a Temporal activity, so an exception thrown from execute() is retried by default. Throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, ...) for errors that a retry won't fix, such as missing configuration or a disconnected port. You can pass empty strings for workflowId and nodeId. The existing nodes do the same.
Call nodeProgressCallback.report(percent) with a value from 0 to 100 as you go. The workbench uses it to show live progress on the node.

Step 4 of 944% through the guide Each node has a Markdown help page that the workbench shows next to it. It's loaded from the classpath on startup, at a path that matches the node's package and class name exactly: src/main/resources/org/projectcontinuum/feature/demo/node/WordCounterNodeModel.doc.md If the file is missing, the node still works, but its help page reads "Documentation not found for WordCounterNodeModel". A good help page covers what the node does, its ports, a properties table, and a small input/output example. See the .doc.md files in continuum-feature-base for the house style.

Step 5 of 956% through the guide execute() only depends on its arguments, so you can test it with Mockito mocks and no Spring context: src/test/kotlin/org/projectcontinuum/feature/demo/node/WordCounterNodeModelTest.kt class WordCounterNodeModelTest { private val outputWriter = mock<NodeOutputWriter>() private val portWriter = mock<NodeOutputWriter.OutputPortWriter>() private val node = WordCounterNodeModel(jacksonObjectMapper()) @BeforeEach fun setUp() { whenever(outputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("data")).thenReturn(portWriter) } @Test fun `counts words and preserves original columns`() { val reader = mockReader(listOf(mapOf("id" to 1, "text" to "the quick brown fox"))) node.execute(mapOf("inputCol" to "text", "outputCol" to "word_count"), mapOf("data" to reader), outputWriter, mock()) val rows = argumentCaptor<Map<String, Any>>() verify(portWriter).write(any(), rows.capture()) assertEquals(4, rows.firstValue["word_count"]) assertEquals(1, rows.firstValue["id"]) } private fun mockReader(rows: List<Map<String, Any>>): NodeInputReader { val iterator = rows.iterator() return mock<NodeInputReader>().also { r -> whenever(r.read()).thenAnswer { if (iterator.hasNext()) iterator.next() else null } whenever(r.getRowCount()).thenReturn(rows.size.toLong()) } } } The imports come from org.junit.jupiter.api, org.mockito.kotlin, kotlin.test and tools.jackson.module.kotlin.jacksonObjectMapper. The feature plugin already adds all of them as test dependencies. These tests call execute() directly, so they skip the schema validation step. To test validation too, build a ContinuumWorkflowModel.Node and call node.run(...) instead.

Step 6 of 967% through the guide worker/build.gradle.kts plugins { id("org.projectcontinuum.worker") } group = "org.projectcontinuum.app.worker.demo" description = "Continuum Feature Demo Worker" version = property("featureVersion").toString() continuum { continuumVersion.set(property("continuumPlatformVersion").toString()) // Optional: set this to build a container image with `./gradlew :worker:jib` // jibToImage.set("docker.io/your-org/continuum-feature-demo:${version}") } dependencies { implementation(project(":features:continuum-feature-demo")) } worker/src/main/kotlin/org/projectcontinuum/app/worker/demo/App.kt package org.projectcontinuum.app.worker.demo import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication import org.springframework.boot.runApplication @SpringBootApplication class App fun main(args: Array<String>) { runApplication<App>(*args) } worker/src/main/resources/application.yaml spring.application.name: continuum-feature-demo-worker # The worker runs a web server. Its default port 8080 clashes with # continuum-api-server in the local stack. server.port: ${SERVER_PORT:8090} spring: temporal: namespace: ${TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE:default} connection: target: ${TEMPORAL_SERVER_ADDRESS:localhost:7233} workersAutoDiscovery: packages: - org.projectcontinuum.core.worker.starter continuum.core: worker: # Every worker needs its OWN task queue (see the warning below). node-task-queue: ${CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE:CONTINUUM_FEATURE_DEMO_TASK_QUEUE} logging: level: root: error org.projectcontinuum.core.worker: info org.projectcontinuum.feature.demo: debug Give every worker a unique task queue If node-task-queue isn't set, a worker listens on the shared default queue ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE. When two workers share a queue, Temporal can send a node to a worker that doesn't have it, and the node fails. Every shipped worker sets its own queue (for example CONTINUUM_FEATURE_BASE_TASK_QUEUE), and yours must too. The worker sends its queue name in its registration message, so the orchestrator knows where to route your nodes.

You don't need to configure Kafka, MinIO, the API server or the credentials server here. continuum-worker-springboot-starter ships defaults that point at the local stack ports, and each one can be overridden with an environment variable: Variable Default Purpose TEMPORAL_SERVER_ADDRESS localhost:7233 Temporal frontend CONTINUUM_KAFKA_MAIN_BROKER_LIST localhost:39092,localhost:39093,localhost:39094 Kafka brokers for node registration CONTINUUM_KAFKA_MAIN_SCHEMA_REGISTRY http://localhost:38080 Avro schema registry CONTINUUM_MINIO_ENDPOINT http://localhost:39000 Object store for Parquet inputs and outputs CONTINUUM_MINIO_USERNAME / _PASSWORD minioadmin / minioadmin MinIO credentials CONTINUUM_API_SERVER_BASE_URL http://localhost:8080 API server CONTINUUM_CREDENTIALS_SERVER_BASE_URL http://localhost:8083 Only used by nodes that call getCredential() CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE none (falls back to ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE) This worker's Temporal task queue CONTINUUM_CACHE_STORAGE_PATH ./.continuum-cache/workflow-data Local staging folder for Parquet files

Step 7 of 978% through the guide ./gradlew build This compiles every module, runs validateContinuumNodeAnnotations, runs the unit tests and builds worker/build/libs/worker-<version>.jar. To check that the annotation guard works, swap @ContinuumNode for @Component and run ./gradlew classes. The build fails with: > Task :features:continuum-feature-demo:validateContinuumNodeAnnotations FAILED Continuum Node Annotation Validation Failed The following classes implement ContinuumNodeModel but are missing the @ContinuumNode annotation:

Step 8 of 989% through the guide Start the platform with the Local Setup compose file and wait until every service is healthy. Start your worker: ./gradlew :worker:bootRun Check that the worker loaded your node. This endpoint returns the node tree that the worker serves: curl http://localhost:8090/api/v1/node-repo Open the workbench. Word Counter appears under the Demo category. Drop it onto the canvas after a node that outputs a text column, such as Create Table, and run the workflow.

documents.t: Step 9 of 9100% through the guide Container image: set jibToImage in worker/build.gradle.kts and run ./gradlew :worker:jib. Jib reads registry credentials from DOCKER_REPO_USERNAME / DOCKER_REPO_PASSWORD. The base image defaults to eclipse-temurin:21-jre and can be changed with jibFromImage. Kubernetes: deploy the worker as its own release in the platform's namespace and set the environment variables from Step 6, including a unique CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE. The charts in the existing feature repos (for example continuum-feature-base/charts/) are a working reference. See Deployment. Publishing feature modules: the plugins configure Maven Central publishing through JReleaser by default. If you don't publish libraries, set publishToMavenCentral.set(false) in the continuum { } block.

Symptom Cause and fix Plugin [id: 'org.projectcontinuum.worker', version: '…'] was not found That version isn't on Maven Central (for example an old -SNAPSHOT), or mavenCentral() is missing from pluginManagement.repositories. Use a released continuumPlatformVersion. See Step 1. Unresolved reference 'databind' / 'ObjectMapper' You're using Jackson 2 imports (com.fasterxml.jackson.*). Switch to tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference and tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper. validateContinuumNodeAnnotations FAILED A class extends ProcessNodeModel or TriggerNodeModel without @ContinuumNode. Worker starts but your node isn't listed The AutoConfiguration.imports file is missing or points at the wrong class, or the node is outside the AutoConfigure package. See Step 2. Port 8080 was already in use on bootRun The local API server already uses 8080. Set server.port (see Step 6). Node fails at random, or runs on the wrong worker Several workers share a task queue. Set a unique CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE. IllegalArgumentException: Unsupported type while writing A cell value isn't one of the supported types. Help page reads "Documentation not found" The .doc.md path doesn't match the node's package and class name. See Step 4.

continuum-feature-base ships 16 production-ready nodes for data transformation, filtering, aggregation, REST integration, scripting, and anomaly detection. 16 nodesKotlin / Spring BootData · Transform · Filter · REST · Scripting Category Node Description Data Create Table Creates a structured table from FreeMarker template configuration Data Column Join Joins two columns from left and right tables into one output column Data Joint Node Joins input strings into one Data Join on Multiple Keys Performs inner join on two tables using two key columns from each table Transform Pivot Columns Pivots table so pivot column values become new columns with value column as cell values Transform JSON Exploder Parses JSON strings and flattens keys into new columns Transform Column Splitter Splits a column into two parts Transform Kotlin Script Runs a Kotlin script for each row, adding a script_result column Filter Dynamic Row Filter Filters rows where the specified column value is greater than the threshold Filter Conditional Splitter Splits rows into two outputs based on threshold comparison Aggregation Time Window Aggregator Aggregates values into time windows, summing by window buckets Aggregation Batch Accumulator Groups rows into batches and adds batch_id and row_count columns Text Text Normalizer Normalizes text by trimming, lowercasing, and removing non-alphanumeric characters Security Crypto Hasher Generates SHA-256 hash of column values Analytics Anomaly Detector (Z-Score) Detects outliers using Z-score method (flags values with |Z| > 2) Integration REST Client Makes HTTP requests for each row using FreeMarker templated URLs and payloads See the continuum-feature-base README for build instructions and dependencies.

continuum-feature-cheminformatics ships 38 production-grade cheminformatics nodes across 10 categories, powered by RDKit. Built for computational chemistry, medicinal chemistry, and drug discovery teams who need scalable, reproducible molecular processing pipelines — parse, standardize, fingerprint, filter, react, and visualize molecules at scale. 38 nodes10 categoriesPowered by RDKit

Category Example nodes Calculators Calculate Charges, Descriptor Calculation (up to 41 descriptors) Converters Canonical SMILES, InChI ↔ Molecule, Molecule Writer, SMILES Parser Experimental Molecule Catalog Filter (PAINS/BRENK/NIH/ZINC), R-Group Decomposition, Structure Normalizer Fingerprints Fingerprint (9 algorithms), Count-Based Fingerprint, Fingerprint Similarity, Diversity Picker Fragments Molecule Fragmenter, Molecule Extractor, Murcko Scaffold Geometry Add Conformers, Add Coordinates, Optimize Geometry (MMFF94/UFF), Open 3D Alignment, RMSD Filter Modifiers Add/Remove Hydrogens, Aromatize, Kekulize, Salt Stripper Reactions Chemical Transformation, One/Two Component Reaction (SMARTS-based) Rendering RDKit to SVG Searching Substructure Filter/Counter, Functional Group Filter, Maximum Common Substructure Plus a Testing node (SDF Difference Checker) for validating molecular data pipelines.

Algorithm Type Typical use case Morgan (ECFP) Circular General-purpose similarity, QSAR, virtual screening FeatMorgan (FCFP) Circular (pharmacophoric) Pharmacophore-aware similarity AtomPair Topological Scaffold hopping, diversity analysis Torsion Topological Conformational similarity RDKit Path-based Substructure-oriented similarity Avalon Substructure Fast screening, patent searching Layered Path-based (layered) Similarity with tunable abstraction layers MACCS Structural keys (166-bit) Quick pharmacophore screening Pattern Substructure Substructure matching fingerprints

Physicochemical (AMW, SlogP, TPSA...), hydrogen bonding, structural counts, stereochemistry, ring systems, complexity, connectivity (Chi), and shape (Kier) descriptors — all computable in a single node pass.
The Molecule Catalog Filter node screens compounds against PAINS (assay interference), BRENK (unstable/reactive motifs), NIH (MLSMR exclusion filters), and ZINC (drug-likeness filters).

SMILES Parser --> Salt Stripper --> Structure Normalizer --> Canonical SMILES --> Descriptor Calculation A typical compound library standardization pipeline: parse raw structures, strip salts, normalize, canonicalize, then compute descriptors — each step a versioned, reconfigurable node. See the continuum-feature-cheminformatics README for the full node reference and more pipeline patterns (hit triage, virtual screening, 3D modeling prep).

The continuum-local-setup repo gives you a single docker compose up that launches the complete Project Continuum stack — infrastructure services, platform backend, browser IDE, and feature workers — all wired together and ready to go. 🐳 Docker onlyNo builds No builds. No cloning five repos. Just Docker.
🐳Docker 20.10+ 🧩Docker Compose v2.0+ 🧠RAM 8 GB available for containers 💾Disk ~5 GB for images + volumes

Clone the repo and start the stack: git clone https://github.com/projectcontinuum-org/continuum-local-setup.git cd continuum-local-setup/docker docker compose up -d Verify everything is running: docker compose ps All services should show running (the temporal-search-attributes-init container exits after setup — that's expected). Open the Continuum Workbench. Example workflows are pre-loaded under /home/node/example-workflows/. Stop everything: docker compose down # keep data docker compose down -v # also remove volumes
The compose stack has three layers: infrastructure, platform services, and feature workers.

Service Port Purpose PostgreSQL 35432 Database backing Temporal's workflow state and history Temporal 7233 Durable workflow execution engine — orchestrates node-by-node execution, handles retries and crash recovery Temporal UI localhost:38081 Inspect running workflows, view execution history, debug Kafka (3-node KRaft cluster) 39092–39094 Carries real-time node execution events from workers to the browser Schema Registry localhost:38080 Avro schemas for Kafka messages Kafka UI localhost:38082 Browse Kafka topics, messages, consumer groups Mosquitto 31883 (TCP), 31884 (WS) MQTT broker — last hop pushing execution events to the browser over WebSockets MinIO localhost:39000 (API), localhost:39001 (Console) S3-compatible storage for Parquet data files passed between nodes

Service Port Purpose continuum-api-server localhost:8080 REST API — workflows, node registry, execution trigger. Single entry point for the workbench UI continuum-message-bridge — Kafka-to-MQTT bridge for live browser updates continuum-workbench localhost:3002 Browser IDE — Eclipse Theia + React Flow canvas

Service Nodes Purpose continuum-feature-base 16 nodes Core analytics — table ops, filtering, REST, scripting, anomaly detection continuum-feature-cheminformatics RDKit nodes Molecular descriptors and cheminformatics operations Want AI nodes? Add the continuum-feature-ai worker image to the compose file for LLM fine-tuning with Unsloth.

The docker/example-workflows/ directory is mounted into the workbench container: 📡SensorDataPipeline.cwf IoT sensor data → anomaly detection → conditional routing → batch alerts via REST 📈AnomalyDetector.cwf Z-score anomaly detection with conditional splitting 🌐RESTNode.cwf Making HTTP requests to external APIs from a workflow 🤖Unsloth.cwf LLM fine-tuning configuration (requires the AI worker)

Containers keep restarting? Check logs: docker compose logs <service-name> --tail 100 Temporal not starting? PostgreSQL needs to be healthy first — give it 30–60 seconds on first run. Workbench shows connection errors? The API server may still be starting. Wait until docker compose ps shows all services as running. Out of memory? Kafka + Temporal + all services need ~6–8 GB. Increase Docker's memory limit in Docker Desktop settings. See the full continuum-local-setup README for more detail.

Project Continuum is an open-source, browser-native visual workflow platform — inspired by KNIME, built for the cloud. You design workflows as a drag-and-drop graph of nodes, and the platform runs them durably: a crashed worker, a dead Kafka broker, or a dropped connection doesn't lose your progress. Apache 2.0Browser-native IDEPowered by TemporalParquet data passing No desktop install — the entire IDE runs in your browser.

🖥️Browser-native canvas A full IDE experience (Eclipse Theia + React Flow) with zero install. 🛡️Crash-proof execution Powered by Temporal, workflows survive process crashes, network failures, and restarts. Every step retries automatically. ⚡Real-time streaming Watch workflows execute step-by-step. Kafka streams events to your browser via MQTT over WebSockets. No polling, no refresh. 🧱Columnar data passing Nodes exchange Apache Parquet tables, not JSON blobs. Fast, compressed, query-ready. 🧩Extensible by design Add capabilities by deploying new worker services, not by modifying existing ones. Zero downtime, zero coupling. 🔓Open source Apache 2.0 licensed, from the workbench to the workers.

A workflow is a directed graph of nodes. Each node runs as a Temporal activity dispatched to whichever feature worker registered it — base analytics, cheminformatics, AI/ML, or your own custom worker. See Architecture Overview for the full execution path.
